p: Sickles ordered Berdan to find out.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: The 1st US Sharpshooters moved into the woods in skirmish order — open files, each man moving independently, using cover. No solid lines. No drumbeats. Just green-coated men filtering into the dark trees.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: The firefight was sharp and brief. The sharpshooters fell back with their information: there were Confederate infantry on Seminary Ridge, south of town, already in position. Longstreet's corps was there.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Berdan returned with his report. Sickles had what he needed.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Whether the reconnaissance actually showed what Sickles claimed it showed — a Confederate flanking movement about to swing around his left — is a matter historians still debate. What is certain is that Sickles used it as justification for advancing his entire corps to the Emmitsburg Road without orders. Whether Berdan's intelligence warranted that response, and whether the advance saved or nearly destroyed the Army of the Potomac, has been argued for 160 years.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Gouverneur Warren stood on the summit of Little Round Top and understood in an instant what was about to happen.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Vincent and Little Round Top”, paragraph 1 of 10

p: The hill was empty. Below and to the south, through his field glasses, he could see the glint of sunlight on rifle barrels and bayonets — Law's Confederate division moving through the trees at the base of Big Round Top, angling toward the rocky slope where Warren stood alone.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Vincent and Little Round Top”, paragraph 2 of 10

p: If the Confederates took Little Round Top, their artillery would command the entire Union line on Cemetery Ridge from the south. The army would have to retreat or be destroyed. Warren sent aides galloping in every direction: get troops, any troops, get them up this hill now.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Vincent and Little Round Top”, paragraph 3 of 10

p: The first aide found Colonel Strong Vincent commanding his brigade on the road below. Vincent did not wait for formal orders — he did not have time for formal orders. 'I will take the responsibility of taking my brigade there,' he told the aide, and immediately led his four regiments up the rocky face of Little Round Top.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Vincent and Little Round Top”, paragraph 4 of 10

p: Vincent placed his regiments himself, walking the ground with quick precision: 16th Michigan on the right, 44th New York in the center, 83rd Pennsylvania center-left, 20th Maine on the extreme left. He was explicit about the left: 'This is the left of the Union line. You must hold this ground at all costs.'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Vincent and Little Round Top”, paragraph 5 of 10

p: He said this to Colonel Joshua Chamberlain of the 20th Maine.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Vincent and Little Round Top”, paragraph 6 of 10

p: Within minutes of the last regiment reaching its position, Confederate infantry appeared at the base of the slope.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Vincent and Little Round Top”, paragraph 7 of 10

p: Vincent was shot through the groin late in the afternoon while trying to rally the 16th Michigan. His men carried him from the field. He lingered for five days. On July 7, as he was dying, word came that he had been promoted to brigadier general. Those around him told him the news. He smiled.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Vincent and Little Round Top”, paragraph 8 of 10

p: 'Did I not tell you that I would be a general officer before the battle was over?' he said.
